variants.title: Justify the channel
variants.context: Choose the simplest live transport that fits: WebSocket when both sides send independent events or binary frames matter; Server-Sent Events for one ordered server-to-browser text stream; polling when updates are infrequent or stateless infrastructure matters.
variants.prompt: A stock ticker page only receives price updates; the user never sends anything live. Which transport?
options: Server-Sent Events, one-way from the server.
A WebSocket, open in both directions.
Long polling on a repeated request.
optionFeedback: One ordered server-to-browser text stream with built-in event IDs and reconnection.
Full duplex adds state the page does not need.
Prices update too often for polling to be efficient.
variants.hint: Does the client need to send live messages?
variants.explanation: Do not choose WebSocket only to reduce headers; measure direction and freshness.

variants.title: Justify the channel
variants.context: Choose the simplest live transport that fits: WebSocket when both sides send independent events or binary frames matter; Server-Sent Events for one ordered server-to-browser text stream; polling when updates are infrequent or stateless infrastructure matters.
variants.prompt: An order-status page changes a few times per hour, and the platform prefers stateless infrastructure. Which transport?
options: A WebSocket held open per page.
optionFeedback: Low update frequency and stateless infrastructure favour request-driven checks.
A persistent connection per idle page is wasted state.
SSE is reasonable, but the stated preference for stateless infrastructure tips it to polling.
variants.hint: How often does the data change, and what does the infrastructure prefer?
variants.explanation: Polling is a legitimate choice when freshness needs are low.

variants.title: Justify the channel
variants.context: Choose the simplest live transport that fits: WebSocket when both sides send independent events or binary frames matter; Server-Sent Events for one ordered server-to-browser text stream; polling when updates are infrequent or stateless infrastructure matters.
variants.prompt: A multiplayer game sends binary state from both client and server many times per second. Which transport?
optionFeedback: Polling cannot deliver sub-second bidirectional updates.
SSE is one-way text, so the client half needs a second channel.
variants.hint: Both sides send, and frames are binary.
variants.explanation: WebSocket earns its persistent-state obligations when the product needs full duplex.

variants.title: Establish the connection
variants.context: Establish a trusted connection in order: secure the HTTP request with TLS and bounds, authenticate and check origin, negotiate subprotocol and capability, admit into a gateway shard under quotas, then return the 101 upgrade with a traceable connection ID.
variants.prompt: A browser opens a chat socket. Put the server’s admission steps in order.

items.text: Return the 101 upgrade with one traceable connection ID.
Negotiate the WebSocket version, subprotocol, and compression policy.
Use wss, validate transport policy, and bound header size and handshake time.
Authenticate the user and check the browser origin.
Enforce account, IP, tenant, and total connection quotas before allocating state.

variants.hint: No persistent state is allocated before admission succeeds.
variants.explanation: Secure → authenticate → negotiate → admit under quotas → upgrade. Reauthorize sensitive operations later; identity can change after the handshake.

variants.title: Establish the connection
variants.context: Establish a trusted connection in order: secure the HTTP request with TLS and bounds, authenticate and check origin, negotiate subprotocol and capability, admit into a gateway shard under quotas, then return the 101 upgrade with a traceable connection ID.
variants.prompt: An attacker floods handshake attempts. Put the defensive order of operations in order.

items.text: Reject requests whose origin or credentials fail.
Rate-limit attempts and bound authentication work at the TLS boundary.
Only then complete the upgrade and allocate connection state.
Apply per-IP and per-tenant quotas.
Reject unsupported subprotocols before any allocation.

variants.explanation: Handshake abuse is contained by rejecting early and allocating late.

variants.title: Establish the connection
variants.context: Establish a trusted connection in order: secure the HTTP request with TLS and bounds, authenticate and check origin, negotiate subprotocol and capability, admit into a gateway shard under quotas, then return the 101 upgrade with a traceable connection ID.
variants.prompt: A device connects with a long-lived secret. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Admit into a gateway shard within the tenant’s connection quota.
Bind device and tenant identity without putting the secret in a logged query string.
Complete the upgrade and attach the connection ID to telemetry.
Accept only the supported message-schema family.
Terminate TLS and bound the handshake.

variants.hint: Secrets do not belong in URLs that get logged.
variants.explanation: Identity binding happens before capability and admission; telemetry starts at the upgrade.

variants.title: Apply backpressure
variants.context: An open connection can accept work faster than a client can consume it. Apply backpressure per connection and topic: coalesce replaceable state, drop only explicitly replaceable events with a resync signal, disconnect persistently slow peers with a typed reason, resync from a snapshot.
variants.prompt: A slow client falls behind on cursor-position updates from collaborators. What should the gateway do with its queue?
options: Coalesce to the newest position per collaborator.
Queue every update without a limit.
optionFeedback: Disconnect is for persistently slow peers, after coalescing cannot keep up.
Intermediate cursor positions have no lasting meaning; the newest wins.
Unbounded queues turn one slow client into memory exhaustion.
variants.explanation: Replace queued presence, cursor, price, or position state with the newest version.

variants.title: Apply backpressure
variants.context: An open connection can accept work faster than a client can consume it. Apply backpressure per connection and topic: coalesce replaceable state, drop only explicitly replaceable events with a resync signal, disconnect persistently slow peers with a typed reason, resync from a snapshot.
variants.prompt: The same slow client is now behind on chat messages. Can the gateway drop some?
options: Yes, silently drop the oldest messages.
Yes, drop every other message in the queue.
No; chat messages are durable, so disconnect instead.
optionFeedback: Silent drops hide missed messages from the user.
Sampling durable content corrupts the conversation.
Never silently drop durable commands or chat messages.
variants.explanation: Drop only explicitly replaceable events, with counters and a resync signal.

variants.title: Apply backpressure
variants.context: An open connection can accept work faster than a client can consume it. Apply backpressure per connection and topic: coalesce replaceable state, drop only explicitly replaceable events with a resync signal, disconnect persistently slow peers with a typed reason, resync from a snapshot.
variants.prompt: A gateway’s per-connection queue has no limits. What limits should be set?
options: Limits on messages, bytes, and queue age.
Only a total memory limit for the process.
None, since TCP flow control handles it.
optionFeedback: Three dimensions bound both memory and staleness.
A process-wide limit lets one tenant starve the others.
TCP flow control does not bound application queues.
variants.hint: Which resource does an unbounded queue consume first, and what does it do to freshness?
variants.explanation: Set queue limits by messages, bytes, and age; do not treat the gateway as an infinite sink.

variants.title: Reconnect without gaps
variants.context: Make resume a protocol feature: stable sequence and event IDs, a durably persisted acknowledged cursor, reconnect with backoff and jitter, re-authenticate and replay after the cursor, snapshot on cursor expiry, deduplicate the overlap.
variants.prompt: A client loses its connection mid-stream. Put the resume protocol in order.

items.text: Detect cursor expiry and load an authoritative snapshot before joining live events.
Authenticate again, restore authorized subscriptions, and request replay after the cursor.
Give every replayable event a stable channel sequence and event ID.
Persist the last application-acknowledged cursor where it must survive restart.
Reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, cancelling superseded attempts.
Deduplicate the overlap between replay and current traffic, then mark the client current.

variants.hint: Sequencing and the persisted cursor exist before any disconnect.
variants.explanation: Resume is designed at the protocol level: identity, cursor, backoff, replay, snapshot, dedupe.

variants.title: Reconnect without gaps
variants.context: Make resume a protocol feature: stable sequence and event IDs, a durably persisted acknowledged cursor, reconnect with backoff and jitter, re-authenticate and replay after the cursor, snapshot on cursor expiry, deduplicate the overlap.
variants.prompt: A mobile app returns after a day offline. Put the steps in order.

items.text: It reconnects with backoff and jitter.
The app kept its last acknowledged cursor.
The cursor has expired, so it loads a versioned snapshot first.
Events carry stable sequence numbers.
It deduplicates any overlap and resumes live.
It re-authenticates and asks for replay after the cursor.

variants.hint: An expired cursor means snapshot before live.
variants.explanation: Replay after a long absence is often impossible; the snapshot path must be part of the protocol.

variants.title: Reconnect without gaps
variants.context: Make resume a protocol feature: stable sequence and event IDs, a durably persisted acknowledged cursor, reconnect with backoff and jitter, re-authenticate and replay after the cursor, snapshot on cursor expiry, deduplicate the overlap.
variants.prompt: A rolling gateway deploy closes connections. Put the client’s recovery in order.

items.text: Reconnect within the randomized retry window with backoff and jitter.
Fall back to a snapshot if the cursor is stale.
Deduplicate the overlap and mark the view current.
Rely on stable event IDs already assigned upstream.
Re-authenticate and restore subscriptions, requesting replay after the cursor.
Keep the acknowledged cursor persisted.

variants.hint: The server’s typed close reason includes a retry window.
variants.explanation: A drain sends a typed close reason and randomized retry window so reconnects do not synchronize.

variants.title: Size the gateway fleet
variants.context: Size connection state and fan-out independently. Gateways budget sockets, queues, and handshake CPU; fan-out multiplies bytes by subscribers; reconnect storms are bounded by handshake capacity.
variants.prompt: Each gateway sustains 50,000 connections. Peak is 1,200,000 concurrent users and you need 25% headroom for a rolling deploy. How many gateways?
variants.hint: Multiply peak by 1.25, divide by per-gateway capacity, round up.

mistakes.feedback: That leaves no headroom for draining a cohort.

variants.title: Size the gateway fleet
variants.context: Size connection state and fan-out independently. Gateways budget sockets, queues, and handshake CPU; fan-out multiplies bytes by subscribers; reconnect storms are bounded by handshake capacity.
variants.prompt: A topic has 20,000 subscribers and each event is 500 bytes. How many megabytes does one event fan out to?
variants.hint: Multiply subscribers by bytes per event.
variants.explanation: 20,000 × 500 bytes = 10,000,000 bytes = 10 MB per event. Partition hot topics so one does not traverse every gateway.

mistakes.feedback: That is one copy; fan-out multiplies by subscribers.

variants.title: Size the gateway fleet
variants.context: Size connection state and fan-out independently. Gateways budget sockets, queues, and handshake CPU; fan-out multiplies bytes by subscribers; reconnect storms are bounded by handshake capacity.
variants.prompt: A network flap drops 300,000 connections at once. Handshake capacity is 5,000 per second. What is the minimum time, in seconds, to readmit everyone?
variants.explanation: 300,000 ÷ 5,000 = 60 seconds at best; jittered retry windows spread the storm over that time.
